text: A lighthouse keeper on a remote island promised the fishing families that the lamp would burn every night. One winter the fuel ship is late, and she has oil for ten nights out of the fourteen until it comes. She can burn the lamp at full strength and hope the ship arrives early, or dim it every night so that it lasts, knowing a dim lamp may not be seen in a storm. The families do not know the fuel is short. She wonders whether to tell them, since the news might send some boats out early to fish before the dark nights, and others to stay home and lose their catch.

An engineer inspecting an old footbridge finds a crack that is probably harmless but might not be. The town festival crosses the bridge tomorrow, and closing it means the parade must take a long road around the river. The mayor asks her for a simple yes or no. She has no time to run the test that would settle it, and she knows that if she says the bridge is unsafe and nothing happens, people will trust her less the next time she warns them.

A clerk keeping accounts for a village cooperative notices that a respected elder has been paid twice for the same delivery of grain. It is a small sum, and the elder is poor and old. The clerk could correct the books quietly and say nothing, ask the elder to repay it, or report it to the cooperative's meeting as the rules require. Each choice has a cost to someone, and the clerk is not sure whether the double payment was a mistake or not.

A seed bank receives a request from two farming villages for the last sacks of a drought-resistant wheat. There is enough for one village to plant its whole field or for both to plant half. A half field may not feed either village through the dry year. The keeper of the seed bank promised the first village a share last spring, before the second village's well failed.

Two neighbours share an old pear tree that grows on the line between their gardens. One wants to cut it down because its roots are cracking her wall; the other's late husband planted it, and she wants it kept. A surveyor has measured the wall and says the damage will grow slowly, over years. They ask a mediator to help them decide before the autumn.
